opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we thought about a fair amount. The measure we ended up using in the time horizon work is how long it takes a skilled human, someone with the relevant expertise, to complete the task. And part of the reason is that time has this nice property of being relatively objective and comparable across very different domains. You can compare a software task to a research task to a cybersecurity task on the same axis, which is hard to do with most other metrics.

Human difficulty ratings, where you ask people "how hard is this, on a scale of one to ten" or something, are appealing because they're cheap to collect. But they're pretty noisy and they're really relative to the rater. An expert and a novice will rate the same task very differently, and it's not clear what a "seven" means across domains. Then you have the question of whether it's even capturing the thing that matters for AI. Something can feel hard to a human because it's tedious, or because it requires holding a lot of context, and those may or may not line up with what's hard for models.

Human success probability is interesting, and in some ways closer to what you want. If you take a pool of people and ask what fraction of them succeed, that's a real behavioral measure, not just a subjective judgment. The issue is that it's very sensitive to who's in your pool. If you pick experts, lots of tasks saturate near one hundred percent; if you pick a general population, lots of tasks are near zero. So you lose resolution at exactly the places you care about. And it doesn't extrapolate as naturally. With time, you can say "models can do one hour tasks now, and that's been doubling every so many months," and that's an interpretable, forecastable claim. "Models can do tasks that sixty percent of contractors succeed at" is harder to turn into a statement about real-world impact.

That said, I don't want to oversell time. It's definitely an imperfect proxy. There are tasks that take a long time but are easy in some sense, like just a lot of rote work, and tasks that are short but require a key insight. And we found that our correlations between time and model success are strong but not perfect; there's residual variance that's probably due to things like how messy or underspecified a task is. So I'd think of these as complementary. In practice we did look at some of these alternatives and they tend to correlate with time reasonably well, which is somewhat reassuring, but time ended up being the one that gave us the cleanest, most interpretable trend.

r001.rationale: The response discusses variation between expert and novice ratings, but does not express an expectation that human-based difficulty measures track the intuitive expertise a task requires.

r002.rationale: It mentions relevant expertise when describing skilled humans, but does not say that existing benchmarks capture tasks’ expertise requirements.

r003.rationale: It identifies the choice of people in the success-probability pool as consequential, contrasting experts with the general population and explaining how each affects results.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we thought about a lot. The reason we ended up using time horizons at all is that you want some measure of task difficulty that's continuous and that you can compare across tasks that look very different from each other. And the obvious alternatives are things like asking experts to rate how hard a task is on a scale, or just looking at what fraction of humans actually succeed at it.

Human difficulty ratings I'm pretty skeptical of, honestly. When you ask someone to rate difficulty on a one-to-ten scale or whatever, you're getting something that's very noisy and very dependent on who you asked and what they happened to be anchoring on. Two people with similar skill levels will give you quite different numbers, and the scale isn't really interval-valued in any meaningful way. A seven versus a five doesn't mean the same thing across raters or across task domains. Time is nicer because it's at least grounded in something concrete. If I say this took a skilled person four hours, that's a measurement, not a vibe. It still has a lot of noise in it, and it depends a lot on which human you're using as the baseline, but the noise is at least of a more legible kind.

Human success probability is more interesting, and I think it's genuinely a reasonable thing to look at. The problem is mostly a range problem. For most of the tasks we care about, competent humans succeed at close to a hundred percent given enough time, so the measure saturates. You can't distinguish a task that takes an expert twenty minutes from one that takes them eight hours if both have a success rate near one. And if you try to fix that by imposing time limits, you've just reinvented time horizons through the back door. The other thing is that success probability conflates difficulty with ambiguity. A task where humans fail a lot might be genuinely hard, or it might just be underspecified so people interpret it differently. For evaluating AI you want to pull those apart, because an AI failing on an ambiguous task tells you something quite different from an AI failing on a well-defined hard one.

So my overall take is that none of these is the right measure in some deep sense. They're all proxies for something like the amount of coherent, goal-directed work a task requires, and you pick whichever proxy has the best signal-to-noise for the thing you're trying to predict. For predicting whether current models can do a task, time horizon has worked surprisingly well, better than I would have guessed going in. But I'd expect that to break down at some point, probably as models get good at long tasks that are long for boring reasons and still fail at short tasks that require some kind of insight. And when that happens we'll need something better, and I don't think difficulty ratings or success rates are it. They'll be part of the picture, but you'd want something that tries to characterize what makes a task hard rather than just how hard it is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses difficulty proxies and human baselines, but does not say they track the intuitive amount of expertise a task requires.

r002.rationale: It does not identify existing benchmarks as capturing tasks’ expertise requirements.

r003.rationale: It notes that success rates depend on the human baseline, but does not ask which distribution of people should define them.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re both useful, but I’d be cautious about treating either as a direct measure of difficulty for an AI system. Humans and AI systems have different strengths and weaknesses, so something that’s very difficult for a human can be easy for a model, and vice versa.

Human difficulty ratings also depend on who you ask. An expert might call a problem easy because they recognize the relevant technique immediately, while someone without that background might not know where to start. So those ratings can tell you something, but it’s not always clear exactly what they’re measuring.

Human success probabilities are a bit more concrete. But you still have to specify the population and the conditions: how much time people get, what tools they can use, and so on. If you do that carefully, you get a useful human baseline. I just wouldn’t assume that ordering tasks by human success rate will also order them by AI success rate. That relationship is something you’d want to test empirically.

r001.rationale: It notes that human ratings depend on expertise, but does not express an expectation that human-based measures track the intuitive expertise a task requires.

r002.rationale: It does not say that existing benchmarks capture tasks’ expertise requirements.

r003.rationale: It says human success probabilities require specifying the population, which raises which group of people would define the probability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are both useful things to measure, but I’d be cautious about interpreting either as a measure of difficulty for an AI. Humans and models have different strengths and weaknesses, so a question that a human rates as difficult might be easy for a model, and vice versa.

Human success probabilities are a little more concrete than difficulty ratings, but you still have to specify which humans, how much time they have, and what tools they can use. The probability that a random person gets a question right is very different from the probability that an expert gets it right. And low success could reflect specialized knowledge rather than a need for particularly sophisticated reasoning.

So I’d use those measures to characterize a task and help interpret model performance. But if what you want to know is whether a task is hard for current AI systems, you also need to measure how those systems actually perform.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that human difficulty may not reflect AI difficulty and says low human success can reflect specialized knowledge; it does not expect human measures to track the intuitive expertise a task requires.

r002.rationale: It does not say existing benchmarks capture tasks’ expertise requirements.

r003.rationale: It says human success probability depends on “which humans” and contrasts a random person with an expert.
